channel.title: Dev|Journal
channel.description: Technical blog covering software architecture, backend development, and AI.

item.title: Python Decorators Are Hidden Control Flow
item.description: Python decorators are elegant syntax for wrapping behavior, but they also change a function before it runs. Use them for stable cross-cutting policies, preserve metadata, and avoid hiding important business logic behind a symbol.

item.title: Python Iterators Need a Contract
item.description: Python iteration is wonderfully flexible, but custom iterators still need clear guarantees about exhaustion, restartability, mutation, and errors. A for-loop hides the protocol, not the contract.

item.title: Java Time Is a Domain Problem
item.description: Java time bugs are rarely caused by arithmetic alone. They come from choosing the wrong temporal concept, losing a time zone, confusing an instant with a calendar date, or pretending every day has 24 hours.

item.title: Java Collections Are Domain Decisions
item.description: Choosing List, Set, Map, or a queue in Java communicates rules about order, uniqueness, lookup, and processing. Collection types should express those rules instead of being selected by habit.

item.title: Java equals and hashCode Are a Contract, Not Boilerplate
item.description: Java collection bugs often come from treating equals and hashCode as generated ceremony. Their relationship defines identity, lookup behavior, and whether objects remain findable after mutation.

item.title: Java Package Boundaries Are Real Architecture
item.description: Java packages are often treated as folders, but package visibility and dependency direction can enforce ownership. A package structure that mirrors technical layers alone is usually a map of coupling.

item.title: Dependency Injection Is Not Architecture
item.description: Dependency injection can improve testability and composition, but a container does not create boundaries, ownership, or a domain model. Wiring objects is plumbing, not architecture.

item.title: Java Virtual Threads Need Boring Code
item.description: Java virtual threads make blocking I/O dramatically easier to scale, but they do not remove database limits, synchronization bottlenecks, or the need for cancellation. The winning code is usually straightforward code with bounds.

item.title: Checked Exceptions Made Java Developers Liars
item.description: Java checked exceptions tried to make failure explicit, but they often produced catch blocks that lied, wrapper hierarchies that obscured causes, and APIs that forced callers to handle failures they could not understand.

item.title: Java Records Are About Meaning, Not Less Boilerplate
item.description: Java records are valuable because they declare a value-oriented model with clear equality and immutability expectations. Treating them as shorter POJOs misses the design decision they make.

item.title: Java Optional Is a Tool, Not a Religion
item.description: Java Optional makes the absence of a value visible at useful API boundaries, but using it everywhere creates awkward code, allocation noise, and a second null-like vocabulary that nobody asked for.

item.title: Java Streams Are Not Automatically Clearer
item.description: Java streams are excellent for simple transformations, but forcing every algorithm into a fluent pipeline can hide state, exceptions, and control flow. Readability is more important than collecting method calls.

item.title: Python CLI Tools Deserve Real Design
item.description: A Python command-line tool is an interface used by people, scripts, and automation. Clear arguments, stable exit codes, useful errors, and safe defaults matter more than the cleverness of the implementation.

item.title: Python Logging Is a Contract With Future You
item.description: Python logging should help a future engineer reconstruct what happened, not merely print the author's current thoughts. Levels, context, formatting, and secrets all matter once code leaves a laptop.

item.title: Python Async Is Not a Speed Button
item.description: Python async programming improves throughput when work spends time waiting, but it does not make CPU-heavy code faster or turn blocking libraries into non-blocking ones by wishful thinking.

item.title: Python Generators Are Control Flow, Not Just Memory Saving
item.description: Python generators change when work happens, not only how much memory it uses. They are powerful for pipelines and backpressure, but they can also hide expensive computation behind innocent-looking iteration.

item.title: Python Context Managers Own the Mess
item.description: Python context managers are more than elegant syntax for closing files. They make ownership, cleanup, and transactional behavior explicit, especially when the code between setup and teardown fails halfway through.

item.title: Timeouts Are Part of the Contract
item.description: A timeout is a product and capacity decision, not an arbitrary client setting. Each boundary should define how long it may wait, what happens afterward, and whether the work can still complete safely.

item.title: Health Checks Should Mean Something
item.description: A health endpoint should answer a specific operational question. Liveness, readiness, dependency checks, and business health have different meanings and should not be collapsed into one optimistic green response.

item.title: Temporary Is a Dangerous Word
item.description: Temporary code, configuration, and compatibility paths tend to survive their original emergency. Give temporary decisions owners, expiry conditions, and a removal path or they become permanent architecture by accident.

item.title: Compatibility Tests Are Negotiation
item.description: Contract tests make assumptions between systems visible. They are most useful when they describe a negotiated boundary instead of freezing every internal implementation detail.

item.title: Code Review Is Risk Allocation
item.description: Code review is most useful when it spends attention on behavior, risk, and maintainability. Treating every line as equally important creates ceremony while important design decisions pass unnoticed.

item.title: Inputs Should Have a Lifetime
item.description: Data is not equally trustworthy forever. Inputs pass through stages of collection, validation, storage, publication, and deletion, and each stage should define what guarantees still apply.

item.title: Python Exceptions Are Part of Your API
item.description: Exceptions are not merely implementation details in Python. Their types, messages, and boundaries define how callers recover, how operators debug, and whether a failure is useful or just loud.

item.title: Metadata Is Not Free
item.description: Timestamps, labels, tracing fields, and audit attributes improve diagnosis, but every metadata field has storage, privacy, indexing, and maintenance costs. Collect information because a decision needs it.

item.title: Abandoned Work Is Still Work
item.description: Canceled requests, expired jobs, and disconnected clients still consume resources unless cancellation is designed explicitly. Systems should know when work no longer has a useful owner.

item.title: Rollbacks Are Not a Strategy
item.description: Rolling back an artifact cannot undo every data change, external message, or customer-visible action. Safe releases need compatibility, forward recovery, and a clear distinction between code rollback and system recovery.

item.title: Python Packaging Is User Experience
item.description: A Python package is not finished when its code works on the author’s laptop. Installation, imports, errors, documentation, and upgrades are the product that every user actually encounters.

item.title: Commands Should Be Replayable
item.description: A command that can be recorded, inspected, and replayed is easier to debug, recover, and audit. Replayability requires explicit inputs, stable identity, and careful control of external side effects.

item.title: Limits Are Design
item.description: Every system has limits whether the team documents them or discovers them in an outage. Explicit limits on size, time, concurrency, and retries turn accidental failure into behavior the product can reason about.

item.title: Consistency Is Not Always Correctness
item.description: Systems often trade immediate consistency for availability, latency, or independent operation. The important design question is not whether data is eventually consistent, but which decisions require which guarantee.

item.title: Python Type Hints Are Design Documents That Happen to Run
item.description: Python type hints are not decorative comments for an editor. Used properly, they expose unclear boundaries, make refactoring cheaper, and force teams to decide what their functions actually promise.

item.title: Side Effects Need a Home
item.description: Writes, messages, emails, and external calls become easier to reason about when their ownership and ordering are explicit. Hidden side effects make retries, testing, and recovery unnecessarily dangerous.

item.title: Feature Completeness Is Not Quality
item.description: A feature is not finished when its happy path works. Quality includes failure behavior, permissions, recovery, observability, migration, and the ordinary awkward cases that real users bring with them.

item.title: Ownership Is a Runtime Property
item.description: Ownership is not merely a team listed in a repository file. It appears in alert routing, deployment permissions, data decisions, and the speed at which someone can act when behavior changes.

item.title: Your API Doesn't Need Versioning
item.description: The default approach to API design is to prefix routes with version numbers like /api/v1/ and /api/v2/. In practice, route versioning leads to massive code duplication, client migration paralysis, and complex routing tables. Designing backward-compatible APIs is a much better operational model.

item.title: Audit Logs Should Tell a Story
item.description: An audit log is not a copy of application logs. It explains which actor changed which business object, what changed, and why the event matters later.

item.title: Why We Should Stop Writing 'Smart' Code
item.description: Writing clever, concise, one-liner code is a common developer ego trip. In practice, 'smart' code is a maintenance liability that increases cognitive load, slows down debugging, and confuses your colleagues. Readable code is boring, obvious, and explicit.

item.title: Search Is a Product Contract
item.description: Search quality depends on decisions about language, ranking, freshness, permissions, empty results, and failure. A text box is only the visible part of a much larger product contract.

item.title: Identifiers Are Long-Lived Contracts
item.description: An identifier escapes its original database and appears in URLs, logs, exports, support tickets, and integrations. Choosing one is a decision about stability, privacy, ordering, and future migrations.

item.title: Inheritance is a Relic: Composition Over Class Hierarchies
item.description: Object-oriented programming taught us that code reuse is achieved through class inheritance. In practice, deep inheritance hierarchies create fragile base classes, high coupling, and rigid domain structures. It is time to abandon inheritance and embrace composition.

item.title: Empty States Are Product Design
item.description: An empty result can mean a new account, a successful filter, a missing permission, or a failed dependency. Treating every empty state as “nothing here” hides important distinctions from users and operators.

item.title: No, You Don't Need a Service Mesh
item.description: Service meshes like Istio or Linkerd promise advanced traffic management, mutual TLS, and observability for microservices. In reality, they add massive networking complexity, consume significant CPU and RAM, and make debugging network issues a nightmare. Keep your cluster networking simple.

item.title: Slow Is Sometimes a Feature
item.description: Speed is valuable, but instant responses are not always the right product behavior. Deliberate work, visible progress, and honest completion states can produce a better system than pretending every operation is immediate.

item.title: Incidents Need Better Questions
item.description: Incident reviews are useful when they reconstruct conditions and improve the system. Blaming a person or collecting a generic list of action items rarely changes the conditions that made the failure possible.

item.title: Why MongoDB is Still the Wrong Choice for 99% of Projects
item.description: The 'schemaless' pitch of document databases promised database flexibility and rapid iteration. In reality, your data always has schema. Moving schema constraints to the application layer leads to data drift, write corruption, and slow queries. PostgreSQL is almost always the correct answer.

item.title: Deletion Is a Workflow, Not a Button
item.description: Deleting data affects references, backups, search indexes, caches, audit records, legal obligations, and user expectations. Treat deletion as an explicit workflow with states rather than one irreversible statement.

item.title: The Fallacy of DRY: Why You Should Write Duplicated Code First
item.description: Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) is one of the first design principles programmers learn. But applying it too early creates tightly coupled, hyper-flexible abstractions that crumble under the weight of changing requirements. Write duplicated code until the structure reveals itself.

item.title: Compatibility Is a Feature
item.description: Compatibility is a deliberate product promise, not an accidental property of old code. Additive changes, clear deprecation paths, and honest support windows let systems evolve without turning every upgrade into a negotiation.

item.title: Abstractions Should Arrive Late
item.description: Abstractions are useful when repeated behavior and stable concepts have appeared. Introducing them before the shape is known creates indirection that protects guesses instead of reducing complexity.
